# Zero-inflated count model

In general, a zero-inflated count model is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y_i = y | \mathbf{x}_i) &= \begin{cases} f(0; \boldsymbol{\xi}_i)(1 - p_i) + p_i & y = 0 \\ f(y;\boldsymbol{\xi}_i)(1 - p_i) & y > 0 \end{cases} \\
\log(\mu_i) &= \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta} \\
\log \left( \frac{p_i}{1 - p_i} \right) &= \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\gamma}
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $f(y; \boldsymbol{\xi}_i)$ represents a count distribution with mean $\mu_i$. The vector $\boldsymbol{\xi}_i$ captures the parameters needed to specify that distribution. 

For a zero-inflated Poisson (ZIP) model, for example, $\boldsymbol{\xi}_i = \mu_i$ and $f(y; \boldsymbol{\xi}_i) = \dfrac{e^{-\mu_i} \mu_i^y}{y!}$. 

For a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB), $\boldsymbol{\xi}_i = (\mu_i, r)$ and $f(y; \boldsymbol{\xi}_i)$ is the pmf for a negative binomial with mean $\mu_i$ and size parameter $r$.

## Parameter estimation

Like a ZIP model, parameters can be estimated for a ZINB model by the method of maximum likelihood.

[Previously](https://sta712-f26.github.io/class_activities/ca_25_2.html), we wrote code to compute the log likelihood for a ZIP model. We then used R's `optim` function to maximize the likelihood (by minimizing the negative log likelihood).

Inputs:

* `y`: a vector of the observed values of the response ($Y_1, Y_2,...,Y_n$)
* `p`: a vector of estimated probabilities $p_1,...,p_n$
* `mu`: a vector of estimated means $\mu_1,...,\mu_n$
* `r`: the estimated size parameter $r$ (a single value)

Output: A vector containing estimated probabilities for each observation.

You may find the `dnbinom` function and the [solutions](https://sta712-f26.github.io/class_activities/ca_25_2_solutions.html) to the previous activity helpful.
:::

## Optimizing

We can now use the `optim` function to estimate $\boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}, r$. 

```{r, include=F}
prob_zinb <- function(y, p, mu, r){
  ifelse(y == 0, 
         p + (1 - p)*dnbinom(0, size=r, mu = mu), 
         (1 - p)*dnbinom(y, size=r, mu = mu))
}

log_lik_zinb <- function(y, X, theta){
  k <- length(theta) - 1
  beta <- theta[1:(k/2)]
  gamma <- theta[(k/2 + 1):k]
  r <- theta[k+1]
  p <- as.numeric(exp(X %*% gamma) / (1 + exp(X %*% gamma)))
  mu <- as.numeric(exp(X %*% beta))
  sum(log(prob_zinb(y, p, mu, r)))
}
```

For example, here are estimates for ZINB coefficients with the NMES physician visit data. We initialize estimates of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and $r$ for a negative binomial fit (without zero-inflation) on the data.

```{r message=F, warning=F}
library(tidyverse)
library(AER)

data("NMES1988")
nmes <- NMES1988 |>
  select(visits, hospital, health, chronic, 
         gender, school, insurance)

nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(visits ~ ., data = nmes)

zero_prop = mean(nmes$visits == 0)
beta0 = coef(nb_fit)
gamma0 = c(log(zero_prop/(1 - zero_prop)),
           rep(0, length(beta0) - 1))
params0 = c(beta0, gamma0, nb_fit$theta)

optim_est <- optim(params0, 
                   function(par) -log_lik_zinb(nmes$visits, model.matrix(nb_fit), par),
                   method = "BFGS")

optim_est$par
```

In practice, we can use `pscl::zeroinfl` again, which supports ZINB models as well as ZIP models:

```{r}
m2 <- pscl::zeroinfl(visits ~ ., dist = "negbin", data = nmes)
```

We can compare our output with the output from `pscl::zeroinfl`, and see that the estiamted parameters are very close!

```{r}
# estimated count coefficients
optim_est$par[1:8]
m2$coefficients$count
```

```{r}
# estimated zero-inflation coefficients
optim_est$par[9:16]
m2$coefficients$zero
```

```{r}
# estimated size parameter
optim_est$par[17]
m2$theta
```
